What are the four essential elements of a design pattern?

The four essential elements are: (1) Pattern Name – a handle to describe the design problem and solution; (2) Problem – describes when to apply the pattern and its context; (3) Solution – describes the elements, relationships, responsibilities, and collaborations; (4) Consequences – the results and trade-offs of applying the pattern.

What is the MVC triad and what are its three components?

MVC (Model/View/Controller) is a triad of classes used to build user interfaces in Smalltalk-80. The Model is the application object, the View is the screen presentation, and the Controller defines how the user interface reacts to user input. MVC decouples these objects to increase flexibility and reuse.

How many design patterns are in the GoF catalog described in the notes?
The catalog contains 23 design patterns. They are organized by purpose (creational, structural, behavioral) and by scope (class or object patterns).

What are the three purposes used to classify design patterns?

Design patterns are classified by three purposes: (1) Creational – concern the process of object creation; (2) Structural – deal with the composition of classes or objects; (3) Behavioral – characterize the ways in which classes or objects interact and distribute responsibility.

What is the intent of the Singleton pattern?

The Singleton pattern ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it. The class itself is responsible for keeping track of its sole instance so no other instance can be created.

What is the intent of the Observer pattern?

The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically. In MVC, it is used to implement a subscribe/notify protocol between models and views.

What is the intent of the Factory Method pattern?

The Factory Method pattern defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. It lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses. It is also known as Virtual Constructor.

What is the intent of the Decorator pattern?

The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically and provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality. It captures relationships that support embellishment by transparent enclosure.

What does the Composite pattern do?

The Composite pattern composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies and lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly. It captures the essence of recursive composition in object-oriented terms.

What is the intent of the Strategy pattern?

The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable, letting the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it. In Lexi, Compositors are strategies encapsulating different formatting algorithms.

What is the intent of the Abstract Factory pattern and its alternate name?

The Abstract Factory pattern provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. It is also known as Kit and is most appropriate when the number and kinds of product objects stay constant but products differ across specific families.

What is the intent of the Builder pattern?

The Builder pattern separates the construction of a complex object from its representation so that the same construction process can create different representations. In the RTF converter example, the converter class is the builder and the RTFReader is the director.

What is the intent of the Prototype pattern?

The Prototype pattern specifies the kinds of objects to create using a prototypical instance and creates new objects by copying (cloning) this prototype. It allows adding and removing products at run-time and reduces subclassing.

What is the intent and alternate name of the Adapter pattern?

The Adapter pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface clients expect, letting incompatible classes work together. It is also known as Wrapper and can be implemented as either a class adapter or an object adapter.

What is the intent of the Bridge pattern and its alternate name?

The Bridge pattern decouples an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently. It is also known as Handle/Body. It prevents a permanent binding between abstraction and implementation and ensures changes in implementation do not impact clients.

What is the scope criterion for classifying design patterns?

Scope specifies whether a pattern applies primarily to classes or to objects. Class patterns deal with class-subclass relationships established through inheritance (static, compile-time). Object patterns deal with object relationships that can be changed at run-time and are more dynamic.

What are the seven design problems identified in the Lexi document editor case study?

The seven design problems in Lexi are: (1) Document structure, (2) Formatting, (3) Embellishing the user interface, (4) Supporting multiple look-and-feel standards, (5) Supporting multiple window systems, (6) User operations, and (7) Spelling checking and hyphenation.

What is the Glyph class and what are its three basic responsibilities in Lexi?

Glyph is an abstract class for all objects that can appear in a document structure. Its three basic responsibilities are: (1) knowing how to draw themselves; (2) knowing what space they occupy; (3) knowing their children and parent. Subclasses define both primitive elements (characters, images) and structural elements (rows, columns).

What is recursive composition?

Recursive composition is a technique for representing hierarchically structured information by building increasingly complex elements out of simpler ones. It gives a way to compose a document out of simple graphical elements and its essence is captured in object-oriented terms by the Composite pattern.

What is the role of the Director in the Builder pattern?

The Director constructs an object using the Builder interface and notifies the builder whenever a part of the product should be built. In the RTF converter example, the RTFReader is the Director — it parses the RTF document and uses the TextConverter (builder) to perform the conversion.

What is transparent enclosure in the context of Lexi's embellishment design?

Transparent enclosure combines (1) single-child composition and (2) compatible interfaces. Clients generally cannot tell whether they are dealing with the component or its enclosure since the enclosure simply delegates all operations to its component. This concept underpins MonoGlyph and is the basis of the Decorator pattern.

What are the four consequences of the Abstract Factory pattern?

The four consequences are: (1) It isolates concrete classes by encapsulating creation responsibility; (2) It makes exchanging product families easy since the concrete factory appears only once; (3) It promotes consistency among products by enforcing use of objects from only one family; (4) Supporting new kinds of products is difficult since the factory interface fixes the set of products that can be created.

What are the three key consequences of the Builder pattern?

The three key consequences are: (1) It lets you vary a product's internal representation since the builder hides the product's structure behind an abstract interface; (2) It isolates code for construction and representation, improving modularity; (3) It gives finer control over the construction process since the product is built step by step under the director's control.

What are the five benefits of the Singleton pattern?

The five benefits are: (1) Controlled access to sole instance; (2) Reduced name space by avoiding global variables; (3) Permits refinement of operations and representation; (4) Permits a variable number of instances; (5) More flexible than class operations.

How does the Compositor-Composition split support the Strategy pattern in Lexi?

The split ensures strong separation between the document's physical structure code and the formatting algorithm code. Each Compositor subclass (strategy) implements a different line-breaking algorithm; the Composition (context) delegates formatting to it and can change the algorithm at run-time via SetCompositor. New Compositor subclasses can be added without touching Glyph classes, and vice versa.

What are the two ways to parameterize a system by the classes of objects it creates?

The two ways are: (1) Subclass the object-creating class — corresponds to Factory Method, but may require new subclasses just to change the product class; (2) Define an object responsible for knowing the product class and make it a system parameter — corresponds to Abstract Factory, Builder, and Prototype, which rely on object composition and are more flexible.

What is the difference between a class adapter and an object adapter?

A class adapter inherits publicly from Target and privately from Adaptee (making it a subtype of Target only), can override Adaptee behavior, but commits to a concrete Adaptee class. An object adapter uses composition to hold an Adaptee instance, can work with many Adaptees and their subclasses, but makes it harder to override Adaptee behavior.

What design patterns does MVC use and for what purpose?

MVC uses Observer to decouple views from models (notifying views when the model changes), Composite to support nested views via CompositeView, and Strategy for the View-Controller relationship (different controllers represent different response strategies). It also uses Factory Method to specify the default controller class and Decorator to add scrolling to views.

What are the four participants in the Builder pattern and their roles?

The four participants are: (1) Builder (TextConverter) — specifies an abstract interface for creating parts of a Product; (2) ConcreteBuilder (ASCIIConverter, TeXConverter) — constructs and assembles product parts, and provides an interface to retrieve the product; (3) Director (RTFReader) — constructs an object using the Builder interface; (4) Product (ASCIIText, TeXText) — represents the complex object under construction.

What is the MonoGlyph class and how does it support the Decorator pattern?

MonoGlyph is a Glyph subclass serving as an abstract class for embellishment glyphs like Border. It stores a reference to a component and forwards all requests to it, making it transparent to clients by default. Subclasses override specific operations (e.g., Draw) to add embellishment behavior, realizing the Decorator pattern through transparent enclosure.

What are the two recurring themes across all creational design patterns?

The two recurring themes are: (1) They all encapsulate knowledge about which concrete classes the system uses; (2) They hide how instances of these classes are created and put together. Creational patterns become important as systems evolve to depend more on object composition than class inheritance.

What is the Intersection of Functionality approach for the Window class and its limitation?

The Intersection of Functionality approach provides only functionality common to all window systems. Its limitation is that the Window interface ends up being only as powerful as the least capable window system, preventing use of advanced features even if most window systems support them.

What are the two additional consequences of the Factory Method pattern?

The two additional consequences are: (1) Provides hooks for subclasses — creating objects with a factory method is more flexible and gives subclasses a hook for providing extended object versions; (2) Connects parallel class hierarchies — factory methods are called by creators, and parallel hierarchies result when a class delegates some responsibilities to a separate class.

What is the prototype manager and when is it used?

A prototype manager is a registry of available prototypes used when the number of prototypes in a system is not fixed (created and destroyed dynamically). Clients store and retrieve prototypes from the registry rather than managing them directly, and ask the registry for a prototype before cloning it.

What are the applicability conditions for using the Bridge pattern?

Use Bridge when: you want to avoid a permanent binding between abstraction and implementation; both should be extensible by subclassing; changes in implementation should have no impact on clients; you want to hide implementation completely from clients (in C++); you have a proliferation of classes; or you want to share an implementation among multiple objects while hiding this from the client.

What are the six approaches for selecting a design pattern described in the notes?

The six approaches are: (1) Consider how design patterns solve design problems; (2) Scan Intent sections of patterns; (3) Study how patterns interrelate; (4) Study patterns of like purpose; (5) Examine causes of redesign to see if your problem involves one; (6) Consider what should be variable in your design — focus on encapsulating the concept that varies.

How does MVC decouple views and models?

MVC decouples views and models by establishing a subscribe/notify protocol. A view must ensure its appearance reflects the model's state. Whenever the model's data changes, the model notifies all views that depend on it, giving each view an opportunity to update itself. This allows multiple views to be attached to a model to provide different presentations.

What is the WindowImp class and why is it used in Lexi?

WindowImp is an abstract class encapsulating window-system-dependent code. It is defined to separate the Window class hierarchy from different window system implementations. Using WindowImp, Lexi supports multiple window systems (Mac, PM, Windows, X) without making the Window abstraction platform-dependent — corresponding to the Bridge pattern.

What are the three implementation techniques mentioned for the Abstract Factory pattern?

The three techniques are: (1) Factories as singletons — one instance per product family; (2) Creating the products — concrete subclasses specify products by overriding factory methods, and the Prototype pattern can be used when many product families are possible; (3) Defining extensible factories — adding a new product kind requires changing the Abstract Factory interface and all dependent classes.

What is the relationship between Abstract Factory and Singleton?

A concrete factory is often a Singleton since an application typically needs only one instance of a concrete factory per product family. The notes also state that many patterns including Abstract Factory, Builder, and Prototype can be implemented using the Singleton pattern.

What is the key difference between Abstract Factory and Builder patterns?

Abstract Factory emphasizes creating families of product objects (simple or complex) and returns the product immediately. Builder focuses on constructing a complex object step by step under the director's control, returning the product only as a final step. What a Builder often builds is a Composite.

What considerations make the Prototype pattern the best choice for the drawing editor framework described in the notes?

Prototype is best for the drawing editor framework because it only requires implementing a Clone operation on each Graphics class, reducing the number of classes. Factory Method would require a GraphicTool subclass per Graphic subclass, and Abstract Factory would require an equally large GraphicsFactory hierarchy. Prototype also allows Clone to be used for purposes beyond pure instantiation.

How does the Singleton pattern support subclassing via the registry approach?

In the registry approach, Singleton classes register their singleton instance by name in a well-known registry. The Instance operation queries the registry by name to return the appropriate singleton. This frees Instance from knowing all possible Singleton classes or instances, making it more flexible than placing subclass determination directly in Instance.

How does applying the Abstract Factory pattern to Lexi's GUIFactory support portability across window systems?

By creating widgets only through the GUIFactory interface (e.g., guiFactory->CreateScrollBar()), Lexi's code has no knowledge of the concrete widget classes. A MotifFactory creates Motif-specific widgets; a PMFactory creates PM-specific widgets. Changing the concrete factory at startup is sufficient to switch the entire look-and-feel, without modifying client code.

What is the structural difference between the Adapter and Bridge patterns and what distinguishes their intents?

Both patterns have similar structure with an abstraction delegating to an implementation object. Adapter is a remedial solution applied post-design to make unrelated classes work together by adapting an existing interface to match what the client expects. Bridge is designed upfront to decouple an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently, promoting extensibility from the start.

What are the known uses of the Builder pattern in Smalltalk-80 mentioned in the notes?

In Smalltalk-80: (1) The Parser in the compiler subsystem is a Director taking a ProgramNodeBuilder; (2) ClassBuilder is a builder that Classes use to create subclasses — Class is both Director and Product; (3) ByteCodeStream is a nonstandard builder that creates a compiled method as a byte array rather than a normal Smalltalk object.

Explain the 'parameterized factory methods' variation of the Factory Method pattern.

In parameterized factory methods, the factory method takes a parameter identifying the kind of object to create, enabling one method to create multiple product types. All created objects share the Product interface. This reduces the number of distinct factory methods but requires the caller to supply a type identifier.

How does Abstract Factory relate to Prototype in creating product objects?

Abstract Factory can be implemented using Prototype: a concrete factory stores a set of prototypes and clones them to return product objects. This is useful when many product families are possible, since the factory does not need to be subclassed for each new product type — it is simply initialized with different prototype objects rather than defining new factory methods.

Why does the notes' discussion conclude that Factory Method is the easiest creational pattern to use first, while Abstract Factory offers little improvement in the drawing editor context?

Factory Method is easiest to use first because it only requires a new operation rather than new classes. Abstract Factory offers little improvement for the drawing editor because it requires an equally large GraphicsFactory class hierarchy parallel to the Graphics hierarchy, adding the same complexity without proportionate benefit. Prototype is ultimately better since Clone reduces class count and is reusable beyond instantiation.

How do Behavioral class patterns and Behavioral object patterns differ in approach?

Behavioral class patterns use inheritance to describe algorithms and flow of control, with relationships fixed at compile-time. Behavioral object patterns describe how a group of objects cooperate to perform a task that no single object can carry out alone, with relationships that are more dynamic and can be changed at run-time.

What are the three key security objectives that form the CIA triad?

The three key objectives are: (1) Confidentiality — data must be hidden from unauthorized access, covering both data confidentiality and privacy; (2) Integrity — data can be protected from unauthorized change, including data integrity and system integrity; (3) Availability — data must be available to authorized users when needed. These form the fundamental security objectives for data and information services.

What is the difference between passive attacks and active attacks?

A passive attack attempts to learn or make use of information from the system without affecting system resources (e.g., eavesdropping, traffic analysis). An active attack attempts to alter system resources or affect their operation (e.g., masquerade, replay, modification of messages, denial of service). Passive attacks are difficult to detect but can be prevented; active attacks are easier to detect but harder to prevent.

What are the four categories of active attacks?

The four categories are: (1) Masquerade — one entity pretends to be a different entity; (2) Replay — passive capture of a data unit and its subsequent retransmission to produce an unauthorized effect; (3) Modification of messages — altering, delaying, or reordering a legitimate message; (4) Denial of service — preventing or inhibiting normal use of communications facilities.

What are the five ingredients of a symmetric encryption scheme?

The five ingredients are: (1) Plain Text — the original readable input; (2) Encryption Algorithm — performs substitutions and transformations on plaintext; (3) Secret Key — a value independent of plaintext and algorithm that determines transformations; (4) Cipher Text — the scrambled output; (5) Decryption Algorithm — the encryption algorithm in reverse, takes ciphertext and secret key to produce original plaintext.

What is the Caesar cipher and how is it mathematically expressed?

The Caesar cipher is the earliest known substitution cipher, where each letter of the alphabet is replaced by the letter standing three places further down. Mathematically, C = E(k, p) = (p + k) mod 26, where k=3 for the classic Caesar cipher. Decryption is p = D(k, C) = (C - k) mod 26. The alphabet wraps around so Z is followed by A.

What is steganography and how does it differ from cryptography?

Steganography conceals the existence of a message, while cryptography renders the message unintelligible to outsiders by various transformations of the text. Steganographic techniques include character marking with pencil, invisible ink, pin punctures on selected letters, and typewritten correction ribbon between lines — all making the message hidden rather than encrypted.

What is the DES algorithm and what are its key parameters?

DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a symmetric-key block cipher published by NIST, implemented as a Feistel Cipher with 16 rounds. Block size is 64 bits, key length is 64 bits, but the effective key length is 56 bits since 8 of the 64 bits function only as check bits and are not used by the encryption algorithm.

What are the features of the AES algorithm?

AES features: symmetric key symmetric block cipher; 128-bit data with 128/192/256-bit keys; stronger and faster than Triple-DES; full specification and design details provided; software implementable in C and Java. AES uses 10 rounds for 128-bit keys, 12 rounds for 192-bit keys, and 14 rounds for 256-bit keys.

What is a one-time pad and why is it unbreakable?

A one-time pad uses a random key as long as the message, used to encrypt and decrypt a single message, then discarded. It is unbreakable because the cipher text has no statistical relationship to the plaintext — it produces random output bearing no information about the plaintext — so there is simply no way to break the code. Each new message requires a new key of the same length.

What is the RSA algorithm and what is its public and private key format?

RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is a block cipher where plaintext and ciphertext are integers between 0 and n-1. Encryption: C = Me mod n; Decryption: M = Cd mod n. The public key is PU = {e, n} and the private key is PR = {d, n}. A typical size for n is 1024 bits (309 decimal digits).

What is a Message Authentication Code (MAC)?

A MAC is a small fixed-size block of data (cryptographic checksum) generated using a secret key appended to a message. It is calculated as MAC = Ck(M). The receiver independently computes a new MAC with the shared secret key and compares it to the received MAC. A matching MAC assures the message has not been altered and comes from the alleged sender.

What are the required properties of a cryptographic hash function?

A hash function H must: (1) be applicable to a message of any size; (2) produce fixed-length output; (3) be computationally easy to compute H(M) for any M; (4) be one-way — infeasible to find M given H(M)=h; (5) have weak collision resistance — infeasible to find M' such that H(M')=H(M) for a given M; (6) have strong collision resistance — infeasible to find any M and M' with H(M)=H(M').

What is Kerberos and where was it developed?

Kerberos is an authentication service developed as part of Project Athena at MIT. It addresses threats in open distributed environments where users at workstations wish to access services on servers distributed throughout the network. Its four requirements are: Secure, Reliable, Transparent (user unaware of authentication), and Scalable.

What is X.509 and what is its basis?

X.509 is an ITU-T recommendation part of the X.500 series defining a directory service. It is based on public-key cryptography and digital signatures. The heart of X.509 is the public-key certificate associated with each user, created by a trusted Certification Authority (CA) and placed in the directory.

What are the two types of passive attacks?

The two types of passive attacks are: (1) Release of message contents — an opponent learns the contents of a transmission such as a telephone conversation, email, or file; (2) Traffic analysis — even if message contents are masked by encryption, an opponent can observe traffic patterns to gain information. Prevention through encryption is the primary defense against passive attacks.

What are the two types of two-way attackers in the Network Access Security Model?

The two types are: (1) Hackers — interested only in penetrating the system without causing harm, satisfied simply by gaining access; (2) Intruders — intend to cause damage to the system or obtain information that can be used for financial gain. The model also describes two security measures: gatekeeper functions (login/passwords) and internal controls (antivirus).

What are the five block cipher modes of operation defined by NIST?

The five modes defined by NIST are: (1) Electronic Code Book (ECB) — each block encrypted independently with the same key; (2) Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) — uses XOR with previous ciphertext block and an IV; (3) Cipher Feedback (CFB) — previous ciphertext is encrypted and XORed with plaintext; (4) Output Feedback (OFB) — successive output blocks are fed back as keystream; (5) Counter (CTR) — encrypts counter values XORed with plaintext.

What are the Feistel cipher design parameters that influence security?

The key design parameters are: (1) Block size — larger means greater security but reduced speed; (2) Key size — larger means greater resistance to brute-force but may reduce speed (64 bits is inadequate, 128 bits common); (3) Number of rounds — typically 16; (4) Sub-key generation algorithm — greater complexity leads to greater cryptanalytic difficulty; (5) Round function F — greater complexity means greater resistance to cryptanalysis.

What are Diffusion and Confusion in the Feistel cipher?

Diffusion is a cryptographic technique that obscures the statistical structure of plaintext by spreading out the influence of each individual plaintext digit over many ciphertext digits. Confusion seeks to make the relationship between ciphertext statistics and the encryption key as complex as possible, achieved by a complex scrambling algorithm depending on both key and input.

How does CBC mode differ from ECB mode of operation?

ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key, making it deterministic — identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks. CBC introduces message dependence by XORing each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block (using an IV for the first block) before encryption, making the system non-deterministic and preventing pattern leakage from identical plaintext blocks.

What are the four sub-processes in each AES encryption round?

Each AES round consists of: (1) Byte Substitution (Sub Bytes) — 16 input bytes are substituted using a fixed S-box table; (2) Shift Rows — rows of the matrix are shifted left by increasing offsets (0, 1, 2, 3 bytes); (3) Mix Columns — each column is transformed using a mathematical function (not performed in the last round); (4) Add Round Key — matrix is XORed with the 128-bit round key.

What is the RSA key generation process? Provide the example from the notes.

RSA key generation: (1) Select two primes p and q; (2) Compute n = pq; (3) Compute ø(n) = (p-1)(q-1); (4) Select e such that gcd(e, ø(n))=1; (5) Determine d such that de ≡ 1 mod ø(n). From the notes: p=17, q=11, n=187, ø(n)=160, e=7, d=23. Public key: {7,187}; Private key: {23,187}. For M=88: Encryption C=887 mod 187=11; Decryption M=1123 mod 187=88.

What is the Playfair cipher and its key rule?

The Playfair cipher treats digrams (pairs of letters) in plaintext as single units, using a 5x5 matrix built from a keyword. Rules: (1) Repeating letters in a pair are separated with a filler (e.g., 'x'); (2) Same-row letters are each replaced by the letter to the right (circular); (3) Same-column letters are replaced by the letter below (circular); (4) Otherwise each letter is replaced by the letter in its own row and the other letter's column.

What is the Hill cipher and how does it work?

What is the SHA-1 algorithm input/output specification and its processing structure?

What are the steps of the HMAC algorithm?

What is the Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange algorithm and why is K1 equal to K2?

Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, devised in 1976, allows two parties to agree on a symmetric key without prior shared secret. Alice computes K1 = B^X mod n where B = g^Y mod n, giving K1 = g^(YX) mod n. What are the differences between stream ciphers and block ciphers?

How does the RSA requirement Med mod n = M relate to Euler's totient function?

How does AES differ fundamentally from DES in its cryptographic structure?

AES is an iterative cipher based on a substitution-permutation network, while DES is based on the Feistel structure. AES performs all computations on bytes (treating 128-bit plaintext as 16 bytes in a 4x4 matrix), and encryption/decryption algorithms must be separately implemented since sub-processes run in reverse order. In DES (Feistel), decryption uses the same algorithm as encryption with subkeys applied in reverse order.

Why does the notes state that even MD5 remains secure for use in HMAC despite collision vulnerabilities?

HMAC's security requires an attacker to either compute an output of the compression function with a random, secret IV (brute force with work of order 2n), or find collisions in the hash function when the IV is random and secret. A birthday attack requires 2(n/2) work but also requires observing 2n blocks of messages using the same key — making it very unlikely in practice. These constraints make MD5 still secure for HMAC even given known collision weaknesses.

Why is the simple columnar transposition cipher easily recognized and what enhances its security?

A pure transposition cipher is easily recognized because it has the same letter frequencies as the original plaintext — only the order of characters changes, not the characters themselves. Cryptanalysis involves laying out the ciphertext in a matrix and adjusting column positions using digram and trigram frequency tables. Security is significantly enhanced by performing more than one stage of transposition, creating a more complex permutation that is not easily reconstructed.
